analysis.one_liner: Cuts taxes on capital gains, corporate profits, and large inheritances while creating new tax-free savings accounts.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on January 23, 2008 with 12 Republican cosponsors and never received a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite large parts of the federal tax code. It would let taxpayers switch to a simpler three-rate income tax (10%, 15%, and 30%), repeal the estate and gift tax entirely, cut the top corporate rate from 35% to 25%, cut the top capital gains and dividends rate from 15% to 10%, and stop taxing inflation on assets held more than three years. It would also make permanent every tax cut in the 2001 and 2003 tax laws, fix the alternative minimum tax, expand the deduction for out-of-pocket medical costs for families without employer coverage, create new tax-free savings accounts, and permanently extend the research tax credit. The bill contains no tax increases to pay for any of it.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the largest benefits would flow to households at the top: heirs of the biggest estates (which the estate tax reached only above multi-million-dollar thresholds), investors holding stocks and long-held assets, and profitable corporations. Middle-income families would get real but smaller help — a permanent fix to the alternative minimum tax that increasingly hit them, a wider medical-expense deduction, and new savings accounts whose value depends on having money to save.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy households, investors, and large corporations

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the estate and gift tax for all deaths and gifts after 2008, ending the tax that applied only to the largest estates.
Cuts the top corporate income tax rate from 35% to 25% and the top rate on capital gains and dividends from 15% to 10%.
Indexes the cost basis of stock and tangible property held over three years for inflation, so gains that merely track rising prices are no longer taxed.
Makes the higher alternative minimum tax exemption amounts permanent and adjusts them for inflation, shielding middle-income taxpayers from a tax originally aimed at the wealthy.

Lets households without employer health coverage deduct up to $7,500 of medical costs per person (up to $15,000 per taxpayer) before hitting the income threshold, and lets unused room be added to a health savings account.

Creates new tax-free Retirement Savings Accounts (up to $5,000 per year, tax-free withdrawals), Lifetime Savings Accounts (up to $5,000 per year, tax-free for any purpose), and $1,000-per-year Lifetime Skills Accounts for job training.
Repeals the sunset dates in the 2001 and 2003 tax laws, making all of those rate cuts permanent, and makes the research and development tax credit permanent.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. The bill has no offsetting revenue: repealing the estate tax, cutting corporate and capital gains rates, indexing asset gains, and making the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent would all be deficit-financed, meaning either larger deficits or eventual tax increases or spending cuts elsewhere. The simplified tax option also keeps only a short list of deductions, so taxpayers who rely on other deductions would lose them if they switched.

drawbacks.text: The bill includes no way to pay for its tax cuts; repealing the estate tax, lowering the corporate rate, and making the 2001 and 2003 cuts permanent all reduce federal revenue, and the bill's text contains no offsetting increases.

Estate tax repeal applies to every estate regardless of size, though the tax actually applied only to the largest estates, so nearly all of the revenue forgone would have come from a small number of very wealthy families.
Inflation-indexing capital gains for assets held over three years, combined with a 10% top rate, would move the tax system sharply toward taxing wages more relative to wealth.

The expanded medical deduction is capped at $7,500 per person and $15,000 per taxpayer, and the new savings accounts only help people who have cash to set aside, so the individual provisions reach unevenly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill mixes a few genuinely useful middle-class provisions — the permanent alternative minimum tax fix, the wider medical deduction, and simpler filing — with very large, unprovisioned cuts that concentrate at the top: full estate tax repeal, a 10% capital gains rate, inflation-indexed gains, a 25% corporate rate, and permanent extension of the 2001/2003 tax cuts. Taken as a whole, the distribution clearly tilts toward wealthy households and corporations, and the cost lands on the Treasury with no plan to cover it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative David Dreier introduced the bill on January 23, 2008, with 12 Republican cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, which was its only action.
The committee, chaired by a Democrat, never scheduled a markup or a vote, and the bill received no floor action before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Treasury kept the revenue it would have lost to estate tax repeal and the rate cuts, while middle-income taxpayers also missed out on the bill's AMT fix and medical deduction expansion; the Bush tax cuts remained on their scheduled path to expire (they were instead extended two years later in a separate fight).

for.name: Rep. David Dreier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair and Simple Tax Act of 2008 and gave introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: Rep. Charles Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill, leaving it to die in committee without action.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 original sponsors were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the Democratic-run Ways and Means Committee took no action on it.

industries.industry: Wealthiest households and heirs of large estates
industries.note: Full repeal of the estate and gift tax, which applied only to estates above multi-million-dollar exemptions, would permanently end the one tax that falls specifically on very large inherited fortunes. The forgone revenue comes out of the Treasury that everyone else funds.

industries.industry: Investors in stocks and long-held assets
industries.note: Cutting the top capital gains and dividends rate to 10% and indexing gains for inflation would sharply reduce taxes on investment income, which flows disproportionately to high-income households, at a cost to federal revenue.
Cutting the top corporate rate from 35% to 25% directly lowers the tax bill of profitable companies, with the difference made up through deficits or other taxes and spending.

industries.industry: Banks, brokerages, and mutual fund companies
industries.note: The new tax-free retirement, lifetime savings, and skills accounts would all be held and administered by banks and investment firms, creating new business alongside real benefits for savers who have money to put in.

Expanding the medical-expense deduction for families without employer coverage makes more out-of-pocket medical spending deductible, channeling additional payment to doctors and hospitals while easing costs for uninsured patients.
